Failure not an option for rural KZN principal

By: Lara de Matos | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
How a rural KZN principal came up with a plan to beat the 'blackboard education' odds...

Unique Selling Point:
While the Department of Basic Education's so-called solution to our increasingly dire public education system includes a recent proposal to lower pass rates even further and possibly eliminate maths as a compulsory subject altogether, the principal of a rural KZN school has come up with his own turnaround strategy, aimed at improving results.

Summary:
School Principal Nhlanhla Dube has a thing or two to teach Minister Angie Motshekga:
If your pupils are not meeting the basic required standards of learning, dumbing down the curriculum is not the solution. Instead, the end game should be to implement methods aimed at improving their performance and ensuring they receive an ACTUAL education that will provide them with the necessary skill set to head off into the big world beyond the school playground...



Further information:
As a Quintile 2 school (which means pupils do not pay school fees), a scarcity of textbooks, a lack of other basic educational resources and a minimal government subsidy that often sees him having to dip into his own salary to cover costs for the facility, Principal Nhlanhla Dube of the Amangwane High School in Bergville, KZN, certainly has his work cut out for him.

But despite the enormous challenges facing this rural school situated at the foot of the Drakensberg mountains, Dube managed to beat the odds and obtained an impressive 92% pass rate in 2015 and an 86% pass rate in 2016.

And he is determined that, come the end of this year, ALL his matric pupils will make the proverbial grade - not just in terms of passing matric, but in obtaining university exemptions as well!

So just how has Dube managed to attain such success?

It's all thanks to a turnaround strategy Dube himself implemented, called the 6-4-6 system:

Said strategy requires that pupils be at school at 6am until 14:00 (2pm).
They then have a two-hour break to head home, have a meal and "decompress", before they are expected to be back at school at 16:00 (4pm) to resume classes, which run until 18:00 (6pm).

As principal at the school for the last 20 years, Dube leads by example and leaves his home in Pinetown at 3.30am to ensure he makes to the Bergville school before the 6am bell rings.



Extra Budget Items:
Car hire and possible overnight accommodation, given that the school is situated in the Drakensberg/ KZN.

Press Release:


Report Card: Vaal
It's been a year since Carte Blanche highlighted the problem of pollution from sewage entering the
Vaal River system. Attempts were made to rectify the problem, but it seems the river is currently
experiencing some of its worst pollution to date. Solid attempt or a dismal failure?

Script:


VO1: It’s barely sunrise on a crisp winter’s morning in rural Drakensberg. But for Mfanelo Mbhele and his fellow matric learners at Amangwane High School, the day has already begun…

LINK: With only the most basic facilities, a shortage of textbooks and minimal subsidies that barely cover costs, Principal Nhlanhla Dube certainly has his work cut out for him. But he’s determined not to let circumstances get the better of him - or his pupils.

VO2: Having first joined the school in 1990 as a teacher, Dube set out to improve the school’s overall performance, when he took up the principal’s chair six years later.

UPSOUND:
00:38:34:17
CM: What was your vision when you became principal of the school?
00:39:05:08
ND: My vision was to ensure the school produces learners who are not only going to seek employment around here, but learners who are going to contribute meaningfully and significantly to the manpower demands of the country…

VO3: In a province that recorded the biggest drop in matric pass rates from 2014, and where 19 of the district’s 457 schools attained a 0% pass rate for two consecutive years, fulfilling that vision was no mean feat.

UPSOUND:
00:40:56:11

CM: What is the 646 programme and when did you decide to introduce it?

UPSOUND:
00:41:36:21

… in 2014…

00:43:03:00
… we started introducing the system where, our matric learners would come to school at 6 o clock in the morning, have an extra hour taught to them… then the whole school joins again at half past 7 right up to half past 2… Then they would go out… come back at 4 o clock in the afternoon, stretch for… two hours, then go out at 6 o clock. So it all completes 6 in the morning… 4 in the afternoon and 6 again in the evening.

VO4: It’s a relentless schedule, that sees these students walk the dusty rural roads over an hour each way, put in a full day’s schooling in overcrowded classes that average 55 learners, and head back home at nightfall, where they attend to the demands of their home life…

UPSOUND:
01:29:21:05
Half past six, I arrive at home in the evening…
01:28:20:30
The chores at home they are quite a challenge… I must first do them…
01:29:27:25
… then I study from 8 o clock up until 12 o clock

VO5: Chores include helping with the cooking and cleaning, seeing to his younger siblings and herding the family’s cattle.

UPSOUND:
01:22:36:00
CM: … It’s a lot of time at school. Don’t you think it’s a big sacrifice?
MM: It’s a big sacrifice, but it’s worth it, because we’ll be expecting good marks.

VO6: When it comes to the effectiveness of Dube’s 646 programme, that he has increased the school’s pass rate by as much as 26% speaks for itself. And for 2015 matriculant, Lindokuhle Mazibuko, it proved to be a determining factor.

LINK: Now in his second year of medicine at Stellenbosch University, Lindokuhle Mazibuko is something of a legend within his Bergville community, after becoming the first pupil at Amangwane High School to score 9 distinctions. And his journey to greatness started right here, in rural Kwa-Zulu Natal.

UPSOUND:
Clip 9273:
I wanted to achieve, because I come from a community that is very disadvantaged… from health care, to infrastructure, to education…
So basically, I want to go back to my community and I want to change it…

UPSOUND:
02:25:32:20
CM: How do you feel knowing that one day, Lindo will be a doctor?
Nokuthula Mazibuko: It makes me very happy. I’ve known from his birth that he was going to be something special. He was different from other children.

VO7: And while Lindo credits Principal Dube for pushing him to succeed, it’s his beloved Gogo that he regards as the champion of his success…

UPSOUND:
Clip 9273 - 01:20
… She’s the reason why I push myself so hard, because I want to make her proud… and I want her to see that she raised a good young man…

VO8: Lindo’s story is a model of success that current Amangwane matriculant, Mfanelo, hopes to emulate…

UPSOUND:
Clip 725 - 01:24:36:15
I wish to do as good as Lindokuhle did, because he is also doing medicine and I wish to do medicine next year.

VO9: It’s a level of dedication that calls for everyone to be on board - not only the learners, but their teachers, who also put in the extra hours required of the 646 programme - for no extra pay.

UPSOUND:
02:53:54:01
CM: So why do you do it?
We love the environment, we love the school, we love the kids, we want to just grow and make the best of them and our community.

UPSOUND:
Voxpop - Clip 823
02:54:46:18
At first, I won’t lie, it was challenging…
02:54:15:13
I thought it would be more than I could put to class… because I have responsibilities at home, I have other matters that I do after school…
But since we started 646, we are doing better and better…
… Especially in my department, the science department… We are increasing the percentage each and every year.

UPSOUND:

00:39:27:55

CM: How do you get that commitment from your team?

PD: I had to make teachers realise… the potential that they’ve got… I encouraged team work…

00:40:12:05
I had to lead by example, teach extra hours…

V10: Teaching extra hours is just one of the many personal sacrifices Principal Dube has made over the years.

UPSOUND:

00:48:37:00

CM: What type of challenges does a quintile 2 school face in general?

00:50:04:09

The funding that we get from the Department of Education is … very little… For me to work on the daily maintenance of the school and almost everything that takes place in the school…

I’m only using R345 000 a year. That caters for the 1015 learners who are on campus this year, the 32 teachers, with myself as a 33rd…

00:52:58:42

… when things don’t go well… I don’t go out there and say, guys, there’s nothing I can do - because that’s failure and failure is not the option.

UPSOUND:
00:52:50:29

CM: How do you make ends meet as a school… are you saying that, you… sometimes take out your own pocket?

00:52:58:29

PD:… I’ve gone throughout all these years providing a little bit of funding out of my own pocket…

00:53:32:29
… just so I can provide some resources… even when it comes to… transporting learners…

V11: With his wife and three children based in Pinetown, every Friday afternoon, Dube drives three hours to his home to spend weekends with his family, before hitting the road again at 3am every Monday morning for the drive back to Bergville, where he then stays on for the week.

UPSOUND:
00:57:15:55
We are doing it for the success of these learners so that they see great things out of their schooling…
01:01:20:01
… but I think I’ve done enough… Considering the fact that I am working far away from my family…
01:02:06:04
Very soon, I will be signing off…

V12: As for what will become of the 646 programme after Dube’s departure, remains to be seen. And as he prepares to bid Bergville farewell, Lindokuhle for one, is determined to someday return to his hometown…

UPSOUND:
CLIP 9277 - 03:50
I’m going to do my internship there and do my community service there, and I’m going to be a doctor there…


TEASER:
While government plans to lower pass rates an drop compulsory subjects like maths, a lone rural school principal is turning the approach to education on its head.

PROMO:
As a rural school situated at the foot of the Drakensberg mountains, with minimal resources, the pupils of Amangwane High School are defying expectations, thanks to a pioneering education programme implemented by their principal.
